result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.full_join()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Join this graph with another, linking every node of one to every node of the other. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L34143-L34226){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.full_join(other) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Full join](/assets/graphs/full-join.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="G is a 5-cycle on nodes 1 to 5 and H is a single node, hub (teal). The full join keeps both graphs and adds an accent edge from every node of G to every node of H: five spokes from the hub to the rim. The result is a wheel with 6 nodes and 10 edges, and hub has degree 5." width="100%"} The full join (graph join) $G + H$ is the disjoint union of the two graphs plus an edge between every node of this graph and every node of `other` (in both directions for directed graphs). Joins build classic families from small pieces: a wheel is a cycle joined with a single hub, a complete bipartite graph is the join of two edgeless graphs, and a cone over any graph is its join with one node. They also model two groups with all-to-all contact between them, such as two departments in a fully connected meeting. The two graphs must have the same directedness. Node IDs and labels follow `disjoint_union()`: this graph's nodes keep their IDs, `other`'s are shifted above them, and clashing labels get a numeric suffix. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The graph to join. Neither graph is modified. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph with all nodes and edges of both graphs plus the `n * m` joining edges (`2 * n * m` if directed). Joining edges carry no weight or attributes. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graphs have different directedness. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Built as `disjoint_union()` followed by the cross edges, in $O(V + E + nm)$ time. NetworkX's `full_join` requires disjoint node names (or a `rename=` prefix); EdgeCase renumbers automatically. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A wheel with five spokes is a 5-cycle joined with a single hub: ::: {#79f23a59 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec rim = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(5) hub = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["hub"]) wheel = rim.full_join(hub) wheel.count_edges(), wheel.get_degree("hub") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (10, 5) ``` ::: ::: Joining two edgeless graphs gives a complete bipartite graph: ::: {#1ca4a08e .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} left = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["a", "b"]) right = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["x", "y", "z"]) left.full_join(right).count_edges(), left.full_join(right).is_bipartite() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (6, True) ``` ::: :::
